preserved_objections.basis: Plant phenolics with low volatility cannot effectively reduce moisture plasticization in ethylene-vinyl alcohol polymers as they lack compatible hydrophilic domains to interact with water molecules, evidenced by the referenced barrier enhancement papers which focus on nano-scale modifications and polymer blending rather than additive approaches.

The proposal fails to address critical boundary conditions of temperature fluctuations during distribution which would cause phenolic migration and potential food contamination, as none of the cited evidence addresses thermal stability of phenolic-polymer composites under dynamic temperature conditions.

The referenced catalytic upcycling paper demonstrates that ethylene vinyl alcohol undergoes irreversible deoxygenation when exposed to certain conditions, contradicting the candidate's claim that barrier properties can be maintained simply by adding phenolics without addressing this fundamental degradation pathway.

The candidate provides no evidence that phenolic incorporation improves barrier properties beyond existing commercial solutions referenced in the baseline, with the nanostructured barrier papers showing superior performance through structural modifications rather than additive approaches.

Industrial scale incorporation of plant phenolics into polymer layers would require completely new extrusion equipment and processing protocols, as evidenced by the solution blow spinning paper which demonstrates the complexity of creating functional multilayers, making this economically unviable compared to existing manufacturing.

The testable prediction fails to account for variability in phenolic distribution within the polymer matrix and potential migration into food contents, with none of the cited papers providing standardized measurement protocols for phenolic-polymer composite barrier properties over extended periods.
